name: Yusuf Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, all right. I'll tell you straight, I don't do many of these.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five, out with my father to check the sheep on the hill, then feed the cattle in the sheds in winter. The rest of the day it's fencing, hay, the barley, or fixing the old tractor, which is twenty years old and runs fine. I love the hills at dawn; what wears me out is the forms the government sends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your family.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Stone Cross is 220 hectares, been in my family four generations, with 150 beef cattle, 400 ewes, hay and some barley. I studied agriculture at university, then came home. My wife Leila works part-time at the church school office and does the farm books, and we've got Marco, who's fourteen, and Sofia, who's eleven, and a mortgage from when we bought my uncle's share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised one bit. Every few years somebody in a suit tells farmers the world's about to change, and it never does. I'd say it after church to anyone who asked, and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing for me, and I'm glad. Stone Cross has been in my family since my great-grandfather, 220 hectares on the edge of the hills with 150 beef cattle, 400 ewes, hay and barley. I don't use computers for farming, I use my eyes, and the farm pays well when I run it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do. I'd replace the roof on the old cattle shed next summer, about 25,000, paid from savings because I don't like borrowing. And I'd keep teaching Marco to handle the cattle at weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My worries are cattle prices, the weather and the rules the government keeps adding. AI was never one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rules. What rules bother you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The forms for every animal movement, the inspections, the subsidy schemes that change every two years. My wife Leila spends two evenings a week on the paperwork. If the government left us alone to farm, we'd do it better and cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, Enzo, who's seventy-two and still helps with the sheep every morning. My father would be pleased nothing changed, he never trusted any of it. And Tom, the neighbour's lad who helps us part-time, would carry on too.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because suits always predict big change.
I'd say it **after church** to anyone who asked, and leave it.
think: I think it means **nothing for me**, which I'm glad about.
I farm with **my eyes**, not computers, and the farm pays well.
do: Replace the **cattle shed roof** next summer for about 25,000 from savings.
Keep teaching **Marco** to handle the cattle at weekends.
feel: **Calm**, as AI was never among his worries.
S0.quote: If the government left us alone to farm, we'd do it better and cheaper.
fieldNote: He owns a **family hill-edge farm** and farms by eye, never with AI.
His real complaint is **government paperwork**, which his wife handles.
He hates **borrowing** and pays for improvements from savings.

steps.text: Replace the old cattle shed roof next summer from savings
Keep farming cattle and sheep the same way with his father

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem and they'll sort it out. A cow still has to be fed by somebody. I'd say the same at the mart, where most of us would agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it touches Leila a bit. Leila works three mornings a week in the church school office, and that kind of work is what this picture takes over. But that's a small wage, and she's said she'd be happy to stay home with the farm books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming the way I do. I wouldn't buy any of these gadgets until a neighbour I trust has used one for five years. If Leila's hours went, she'd take on more of the farm paperwork and we'd manage fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's not my world. I'd feel a bit sorry for the young people in offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait five years after a neighbour uses something. Has that ever cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, maybe. I was the last farm round here to get a quad bike, and my father and I walked the hills for years while others rode. But I've also never bought a machine that broke the bank, and three of my neighbours have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Marco about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marco to learn a trade with his hands, like I did, and to never trust a job that sits behind a screen. Marco is fourteen and already handles the cattle better than most men. If he wants to farm, the farm will be here.

say: I'd say it's the **office people's** problem, not mine.
I'd say at the mart that **a cow still** has to be fed by somebody.
think: I think it touches **Leila's part-time** school office job a little.
Her **small wage** matters less than the farm, and she'd happily stay home.
do: Keep farming the **same way** without buying new gadgets.
Wait until a **trusted neighbour** has used a gadget for five years.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **sorry** for young office workers.
S1.quote: I was the last farm round here to get a quad bike, and my father and I walked the hills for years while others rode.
fieldNote: He sees Steady Disruption as **someone else's problem**.
His wife's **part-time office job** is the only household exposure.
His slow approach once cost him **a quad bike**, but saved him from bad loans.

steps.text: Keep farming the same way without new gadgets
Wait until a trusted neighbour has used a new machine for five years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, and that people should slow it down. I don't believe the government will do anything useful, but the companies selling it should be held responsible. I'd keep farming and say my piece at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it hurts us badly by 2031. The big beef ranches will get robots first and push the price of cattle down. I'd still own the land, but the farm might not pay the mortgage, and Marco might have nothing to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but the animals: no new shed roof, no new car. I'd build the savings to two years of costs. And I'd talk to my cousin Paolo, who has a butcher's shop in town, about selling our beef straight to his customers, so we're not at the mercy of the big buyers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I won't lie. I'd be the generation of my family that couldn't keep the land paying, and that keeps me up some nights. My great-grandfather would turn in his grave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI arrives in 2028 and the robots three years later. What does that mean on your farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028, almost nothing, because there's hardly any thinking work on my farm that I'd hand to a machine. It's 2031 that scares me, when the big ranches get robots that work all night. Those three years I'd spend getting the butcher's shop deal going, so we have our own customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the companies should be held responsible. Should the government help farmers like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want a handout, I've never taken one I didn't have to. But if the government lets these companies flood the market with cheap robot beef, it should at least make them label it. People will pay for beef raised by a family, if they know.

say: I'd say it's **madness** and should be slowed down.
I'd say the **companies selling it** should be held responsible.
think: I think it hurts us **badly by 2031**, when robot ranches cut cattle prices.
We'd own the land, but it might not **pay the mortgage**.
do: Stop spending on **anything but the animals**.
Build savings to **two years** of farm and household costs.
Sell beef **straight through** cousin Paolo's butcher's shop.
feel: **Anxious**, fearing to be the generation that **lost the farm**.
S2.quote: I'd be the generation of my family that couldn't keep the land paying, and that keeps me up some nights.
fieldNote: His fear is about **family legacy**, not just money.
He sees the **robot ranches** as the real threat, not thinking AI.
He rejects **handouts** but wants robot-raised beef labelled.
His answer is to build **direct sales** through family.

steps.text: Stop spending on anything except the animals
Build savings to two years of farm and household costs
Sell beef directly through cousin Paolo's butcher's shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like with the fast one, I'd say slow it down. Five years is still fast for farming. I'd say it at the mart and to the parish council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives us time to get our own customers. If Paolo's butcher shop and a few restaurants take our beef by 2031, the robot ranches matter less. I think we'd come through it, though tighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the butcher's deal with Paolo in the next year and see how it goes. I'd hold off on any big decisions until I see what the robots actually do. And I'd talk to Marco about an apprenticeship as a farm mechanic, because somebody has to fix the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it. Five years is time to build something. I'd pray on it, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd talk to Marco about an apprenticeship. Would he want that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would want to farm, plain and simple. But I'd tell Marco this: a farmer who can fix a robot will keep the family farm, and one who can't might not. It's not what I'd have chosen for him, but it's practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pray on it. What role does your church play in this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The church is where we look after each other when things go wrong. When the Bennetts' barn burned down, the whole parish turned out to rebuild it. If robots hurt the farms round here, that's where we'd lean, not on the government.

say: I'd say **slow it down**, because five years is still fast.
I'd say it at the **mart** and to the parish council.
think: I think five years gives us time to **build our own customers**.
With direct sales, the **robot ranches** matter less.
do: Start the **butcher's deal** with Paolo in the next year.
Hold off **big decisions** until the robots prove themselves.
Talk to **Marco** about a farm mechanic apprenticeship.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to live with it.
S3.quote: A farmer who can fix a robot will keep the family farm, and one who can't might not.
fieldNote: With time he would build **direct sales** to protect the farm.
He would steer **Marco** to a mechanic apprenticeship, against his own wishes.
He would lean on the **church community** rather than the government.

steps.text: Start selling beef through Paolo's butcher's shop next year
Hold off big decisions until the robots prove themselves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is better, and we can adjust slowly. But I'd still say there's no need to rush into it. Let people decide for themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I can hand the farm to Marco in good shape. I'd be 56 when the robots come in 2039, and Marco would be 27, old enough to decide what to do with it. I think we'd be all right, if we keep our customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming and keep saving as I always have. I'd build up the direct beef sales slowly over the decade. And I'd make sure Marco gets both his farming skills and his mechanic's training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. It's a long time, and a lot can happen. I'd feel better than with the fast ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your father, Enzo, say about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father would say we've seen worse: the foot-and-mouth years, the droughts, the price crashes. My father's generation survived all of it by sticking together. He'd say robots are just another storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change, even now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more time with Sofia, my daughter, who's eleven. Sofia doesn't care for the farm like Marco does, and I've not paid her enough attention. Whatever happens with the machines, I can spend more time with my daughter Sofia now.

say: I'd say ten years is **better**, with time to adjust slowly.
I'd say **let people decide** for themselves, with no rush.
think: I think I can **hand the farm** to Marco in good shape.
I'd be **56** and Marco 27 when the robots come.
do: Build up **direct beef sales** slowly over the decade.
Make sure **Marco** gets farming and mechanic's training.
feel: **Uneasy**, but better than in the fast pictures.
S4.quote: Whatever happens with the machines, I can spend more time with my daughter Sofia now.
fieldNote: With ten years his focus becomes **handing over** the farm to his son.
He draws strength from his **father's** experience of past crises.
The question makes him think about his **daughter**, Sofia, not just the farm.

steps.text: Keep farming cattle and sheep as always
Keep saving steadily from the farm income
Make sure Marco gets both farming and mechanic's training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to build our own customers before the robot ranches came. What would help is honest labelling, so people know beef from a family farm. And for the government to cut the paperwork so we can get on with farming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land itself. Land is the only thing they're not making more of, and families like mine have looked after it for generations. Robots won't love a hill the way my father does.

headlineQuote: Robots won't love a hill the way my father does.
portrait: Yusuf, 43, owns a **four-generation** hill-edge beef and sheep farm with his father helping.
He **never uses AI** and waits years after neighbours before buying new machines.
He blames **companies and government paperwork**, and rejects handouts.
He goes from **calm** to **anxious** in AGI by 2028, fearing for the family farm.
His answer is **direct beef sales** through family and passing the farm to his son.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as there'd be no time to build direct customers.
whatWouldHelp: **Honest labelling** of beef from family farms.
Less **government paperwork** so farmers can get on with it.
